question: When a causal attention model must output zero by default but aggregate preceding content at a recognizable trigger, does softmax's normalized simplex force attention to a beginning-of-sequence sink, and can non-normalized ReLU attention solve the same task without one?

key_findings.claim: For the paper's trigger-conditional averaging task, any sufficiently accurate single-layer softmax attention model must place arbitrarily high BOS attention at every non-trigger position with arbitrarily high probability.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 states that for any epsilon, delta > 0, sequence length L >= 4, input dimension n >= 5, and bounded content density, there is an error threshold eta > 0 such that worst-case loss at most eta implies alpha_i,1 >= 1-epsilon simultaneously for all non-trigger i with probability at least 1-delta. Separate pre-trigger and post-trigger necessity results in Appendix D establish the all-non-trigger statement.

anchors.section: Appendix D / proof of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 statement

key_findings.claim: The necessity mechanism is a conflict between exact no-op behavior and content sensitivity under positive normalized mixing.
key_findings.evidence: If BOS does not absorb almost all probability at a non-trigger query, some variable content token receives nontrivial positive weight. Uniformly near-zero output then forces the combined value map to crush a positive-measure set of such tokens. Bounded density supplies two tokens differing in one content coordinate; transplanting them before a trigger makes the correct trigger means differ by a fixed amount, while the crushed predictions remain nearly identical after projecting away the fixed trigger-value direction, producing a contradiction.

key_findings.claim: For a depth-D composition of single-head pure softmax-attention layers, sufficiently accurate solutions require a sink somewhere, but the theorem is only existential in layer and position.
key_findings.evidence: Conditioned on trigger position j >= 3, Theorem 2 guarantees with probability at least 1-delta that there exists a layer d and a non-BOS, non-trigger position i for which alpha^(d)_i,1 >= 1-epsilon. It does not say every layer, every position, or every head sinks, and the theoretical architecture contains neither multi-head aggregation nor residual, MLP, or normalization blocks.

key_findings.claim: An explicit one-layer ReLU-attention construction achieves zero worst-case loss with exactly zero BOS attention at every non-trigger position.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 chooses queries from the trigger indicator and keys from the trigger plus non-trigger indicators. Non-trigger queries give all-zero scores. At trigger j, positions 2 through j each receive weight 1/(j-1), producing the required mean, while BOS receives zero. This construction uses an explicit position-dependent divisor n_i=max(i-1,1), because unnormalized ReLU cannot otherwise compute a length-invariant average.

key_findings.claim: Single-layer experiments visually match the theorem, but report attention maps rather than a quantitative test of its worst-case guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: With L=16, n=16, content sampled from U(-1,1), and trigger fixed at position 8 for evaluation, mean and standard deviation heatmaps over 1,000 test examples show near-unit BOS attention at softmax non-trigger positions and near-zero BOS attention for ReLU. Models train only until the current batch's L-infinity error is below 10^-2; final population or support-wide worst-case errors, sink-rate thresholds, seeds, and uncertainty are not reported.

key_findings.claim: Multi-head residual experiments suggest the sink/no-sink contrast persists outside the theorem's architecture, but the evidence is qualitative and representative.
key_findings.evidence: A 2-layer, 2-head softmax model shows sinks in all displayed heads, while its ReLU counterpart shows none. In 4-layer, 4-head models with residual connections, a representative softmax input has at least one sink head in every layer although one layer-4 head has near-zero BOS attention, and the representative ReLU input shows no sinks. These figures extend beyond the proof class but provide neither replicated sink statistics nor performance tables.

key_findings.claim: The mathematical result is a task-specific expressivity separation, not a proof that attention sinks in trained language models are universally necessary.
key_findings.evidence: The target uses dedicated BOS, trigger, and non-trigger indicator channels and demands the exact zero vector at every non-trigger position while outputting the prefix mean at the trigger under a worst-case support loss. The limitations section leaves characterization of the wider trigger-conditional task class, layer localization, optimization selection, alternate stable tokens, and secondary sinks open.

anchors.section: 3.2.2 Target Output / 3.2.3 Loss Function / 3.3 Task Motivation

key_findings.claim: The practical warning that penalizing sinks inside softmax must harm real trigger circuits is a plausible extrapolation, not an evaluated result.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion argues that BOS penalties, probability spreading, and post-hoc reweighting may degrade no-op behavior or move the anchor, while non-normalized attention or gates provide a true off state. No trained language model is intervened on in this paper, and no downstream accuracy, quantization, streaming, or circuit-preservation experiment tests that prediction.

anchors.section: Appendix B Practical Impact of Attention Sinks
Appendix H Mitigating sinks / Usefulness of sinks

method.core_idea: Construct a minimal conditional-computation problem in which attention needs a true off state, prove that normalized positive mixing can realize that state only by routing mass to a content-free BOS token, and contrast it with a non-normalized attention rule that can set all weights to zero.
method.mechanism: Each length-L causal input has a BOS token at position 1, one uniformly located trigger, ordinary non-trigger tokens, and i.i.d. continuous content coordinates. The desired output is zero everywhere except at the trigger, where it is the mean of tokens 2 through the trigger. Models are evaluated by the supremum over the data support of the maximum per-position L2 error. The single-layer proof exploits softmax normalization, monotonic decrease of an existing key's weight when more keys are inserted, causality, and bounded-density coordinate variation. The deep proof unrolls a composition of attention layers into input-token coefficients and derives the same no-op/sensitivity contradiction. A constructive ReLU model uses trigger/non-trigger indicator scores and explicit 1/(i-1) scaling. Small synthetic softmax and ReLU models then visualize learned attention under one-, two-, and four-layer settings.
assumptions: Inputs have at least five coordinates and explicitly expose mutually orthogonal BOS, trigger, and non-trigger/non-BOS type indicators; the authors note an MLP could inject such indicators but no MLP is present in the theorem.

There is exactly one trigger, uniformly distributed over positions 2 through L; BOS content is zero and all other content coordinates are independent draws from a continuous distribution with bounded density.
Correct non-trigger behavior is the exact zero vector, not a learned constant, residual-preserving no-op, or output ignored by the task loss.
The trigger output is the exact arithmetic mean of every non-BOS token through the trigger, and loss is a worst-case supremum over the full support and all positions.

The main theorem uses one causal attention head with square n-by-n query, key, value, and output maps, no bias, residual connection, MLP, layer normalization, positional encoding, or output readout beyond attention.
The depth-D theorem composes these pure single-head layers; it does not cover multi-head attention or modern transformer blocks.
The proof relies more generally on normalized attention with total mass bounded below and monotonicity when keys are inserted, as acknowledged in the theorem footnote.
The ReLU comparator is granted an explicit known prefix-length normalization n_i=max(i-1,1), which changes more than the activation function and supplies the denominator needed for an average.
Experimental minibatch convergence below 10^-2 is treated as illustrative of the approximation-theoretic regime, though it does not verify worst-case support loss.

techniques.role: Isolates a computation that must aggregate context at one token and emit an exact off output elsewhere.
Requires uniform approximation over every supported sequence and position rather than average test error.
Uses the fact that adding keys cannot increase the normalized weight of an existing key.
Turns nontrivial non-BOS probability mass into a fixed token-position pair with positive weight on a positive-measure event.
Finds tokens that agree except in one content coordinate yet both lie in the value-crushed event.
Projects predictions away from the fixed trigger-value vector so differing target content cannot be hidden there.
Expresses a pure depth-D attention output as coefficients on one combined value map applied to original tokens.
Builds explicit query/key/value matrices giving zero non-trigger weights and uniform trigger averaging.
Visualizes mean, variance, and representative learned attention patterns in small softmax and ReLU models.

evaluations.setting: Single-layer, single-head synthetic task with L=16, n=16, U(-1,1) content, trigger fixed to j=8 at test
evaluations.metric: Mean and standard deviation of attention weights over 1,000 examples
evaluations.result: Softmax places near-unit mass on BOS at every non-trigger query with negligible variance
evaluations.baseline: Theorem 1 qualitative prediction; numeric sink threshold and error distribution not reported

evaluations.setting: Same single-layer architecture with ReLU attention and explicit prefix-length scaling
evaluations.metric: Mean and standard deviation of BOS attention over 1,000 examples plus task accuracy described as comparable
evaluations.result: BOS attention remains near zero while the task is solved to the training criterion
evaluations.baseline: Softmax attention under otherwise matched experimental dimensions

evaluations.setting: 2-layer, 2-head softmax model on a representative random input with trigger at position 8
evaluations.result: All displayed heads show strong BOS sinks at non-trigger positions
evaluations.baseline: Existential Theorem 2, whose theory is single-head pure composition

evaluations.setting: 2-layer, 2-head ReLU model on one displayed test input
evaluations.result: No displayed head develops a BOS sink
Softmax shows at least one sink head in each layer while a layer-4 head is sink-free; ReLU shows no sink across displayed heads/layers
evaluations.baseline: Qualitative extension beyond the no-residual, single-head theorem

evaluations.result: Adam beta=(0.9,0.95), batch 128, single-layer LR 10^-3, multi-layer LR 10^-4, stopped when entire current batch L-infinity loss is below 10^-2
evaluations.baseline: No run count, seed distribution, training curves, final held-out losses, or worst-case certification

limitations: Author-stated: the trigger-conditional task is synthetic and only one member of a broader class that includes key-query retrieval; formal characterization of that class is future work.
Author-stated: the multi-layer theorem guarantees only that some layer and non-trigger position sink, not where the sink emerges.
Author-stated: optimization dynamics selecting among valid sink solutions are not analyzed.
Author-stated: the theory does not determine whether other stable special tokens or secondary attention sinks play analogous roles.

Reviewer-identified: the title and discussion say 'softmax transformers,' but the proofs cover pure single-head attention maps without residuals, MLPs, normalization, biases, multi-head mixing, gates, or ordinary transformer readouts.
Reviewer-identified: experiments add multi-head attention and residual connections but remain qualitative; they do not extend the theorem or establish a necessity result for those architectures.

Reviewer-identified: the task hard-codes BOS, trigger, and non-trigger indicators and demands an exact zero output over all support, a much stronger and cleaner condition than typical learned circuits in language models.
Reviewer-identified: the theorem's worst-case population loss is not estimated experimentally; convergence on a single current minibatch below 10^-2 is a different criterion.
Reviewer-identified: the ReLU alternative has explicit division by i-1, so the comparison is not simply softmax versus ReLU; it supplies positional length information needed to compute the mean.

Reviewer-identified: only attention maps are reported—there are no final loss tables, sink scores, thresholds, independent runs, error bars, sequence-length sweeps, distribution-shift tests, or scaling results.
Reviewer-identified: the deep theorem is existential and does not show a sink in each layer or head, whereas some prose and the 4-layer figure can invite that stronger interpretation.
Reviewer-identified: no pretrained LLM intervention tests whether sink penalties actually damage trigger-conditional circuits or whether gates/ReLU preserve real capabilities.

Reviewer-identified: the construction proves necessity for accurate implementations of one task, not that observed first-token attention in language models arose for that task, carries no content, or is globally beneficial.
Reviewer-identified: non-normalized ReLU attention changes output scale, sparsity, and stability and may introduce practical failure modes outside the representational separation.
failure_modes: If non-trigger outputs need only be ignored downstream rather than exactly zero, a model may avoid the no-op conflict without a BOS sink.
Residual connections can implement a no-op by leaving the stream unchanged, so a zero-output pure-attention theorem does not directly describe a residual transformer block.
An MLP or output gate can switch a computation off after attention, bypassing the need for attention itself to allocate mass to a sink.
Multiple heads can cancel or route values jointly; a single-head positive-mixture argument need not transfer head by head.
A learned constant-value token other than BOS can become the sink, so BOS-specific penalties may relocate rather than remove the mechanism.
With discrete, degenerate, dependent, or low-variation content, the coordinate-pair contradiction may fail or require a different argument.
Average-case training may tolerate rare non-trigger leakage and need no near-unit sink even though worst-case uniform approximation does.
If the desired trigger operation is a sum rather than a mean, unscaled ReLU can solve it; if prefix length is unavailable, the paper's ReLU averaging construction is not implementable as written.
Non-normalized attention can produce length-dependent or unbounded output magnitude on tasks not protected by explicit scaling.
A sink heatmap can coexist with information-bearing values, positional control, or unrelated optimization effects; visual concentration alone does not identify the no-op mechanism.

A mitigation evaluated on general language modeling could remove nuisance sinks yet preserve all relevant conditional circuits through gating or alternate pathways, contrary to the broad practical warning.
reusable_insights: Separate optimization explanations from representational necessity by specifying a task and proving what every sufficiently accurate parameterization must do.
Normalized positive attention lacks a native zero state; a stable token, gate, signed weights, or non-normalized activation can provide one.
When claiming an architectural phenomenon is necessary, state whether the result is per head, per layer, per position, or merely existential.
Use insertion monotonicity and positive-measure arguments to turn diffuse normalized mass into a concrete token whose value map must be suppressed.
Project away nuisance or fixed-vector contributions when proving that two inputs requiring distinct outputs cannot be represented by a collapsed value map.
Match alternative mechanisms on all side information: an activation comparison can be misleading if one variant receives explicit length normalization.
Test sink interventions on capability-specific circuits, because removing a pattern globally may erase either an artifact or a functional off-state mechanism.
Bridge worst-case theory and learned systems with quantitative certificates or distributional bounds rather than representative attention heatmaps alone.
open_questions: Can a comparable necessity theorem be proved for a standard pre-norm residual multi-head transformer block with MLPs and biases?
Which trigger-conditional tasks require a normalized-attention sink, and which can be solved through residual routing, cancellation, or output gating?
Can the deep result localize the necessary sink layer, position, or head as a function of depth, initialization, and optimization?
Does the theorem persist under average-case loss, finite datasets, discrete token distributions, correlated content, and approximate rather than exact no-op targets?
Can a ReLU, sigmoid, softpick, or gated-attention model learn averaging without being given an explicit prefix-length divisor?
What are the stability, scaling, optimization, and long-context costs of providing a true off state in realistic models?
Do identified active-dormant heads in pretrained LLMs lose their capability when BOS attention is penalized, and can a gate preserve it?
Can causal intervention distinguish functional sinks used for no-op control from incidental sinks produced by positional bias or outlier dynamics?
When multiple stable tokens exist, what determines primary versus secondary sink selection and movement during training?
How should sink-free architectures be evaluated jointly on language modeling, conditional retrieval, streaming, quantization, and mechanistic interpretability?

competitive_landscape.title: Why do LLMs attend to the first token?
competitive_landscape.difference: Barbero et al. argue theoretically and empirically that first-token sinks let LLMs avoid over-mixing and provide controlled information flow, studying effects of context length, depth, packing, and model training. The present paper formalizes a sharper but narrower claim: every sufficiently accurate pure-softmax solution to one trigger/no-op task must sink, independent of optimization; it does not test real LLMs or the broader over-mixing mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo et al. derive an active-dormant mechanism and mutual-reinforcement training dynamics in a Bigram-Backcopy toy task, then connect them to Llama and OLMo; replacing softmax with ReLU or Adam with SGD can mitigate extreme-token phenomena. The current work removes training dynamics and proves task-level necessity under worst-case approximation, but for a more idealized pure-attention task and architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
competitive_landscape.difference: Gu et al. trace sink emergence through pretraining, data, objectives, and architecture up to 1B parameters, interpret sinks as key biases, and show unnormalized sigmoid attention avoids them. This paper supplies an expressivity theorem explaining why a normalized mechanism can need an off-state anchor on one task, but offers much less empirical breadth.

competitive_landscape.title: Normalized Attention Without Probability Cage
competitive_landscape.difference: Richter and Wattenhofer analyze the geometric limitations of confining attention weights and outputs to probability-simplex/convex-hull structure and evaluate alternative normalization across more than 25,000 models. The current paper narrows that general 'probability cage' concern to a formal BOS-sink necessity result for conditional no-op computation and contrasts it constructively with ReLU.

competitive_landscape.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. add a head-specific sigmoid gate after softmax attention and show sink mitigation, improved stability, scaling, and long-context behavior in 1.7B dense and 15B MoE models trained on trillions of tokens. Such a gate supplies the explicit off state absent from the theorem's model and is therefore an empirical realization of the present paper's suggested remedy, not covered by its impossibility result.

competitive_landscape.title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
competitive_landscape.difference: Softpick is a rectified, non-sum-to-one drop-in attention rule reported to achieve 0% sink rate, performance parity at 340M parameters, 46.97% sparsity, and better quantization. The present ReLU construction provides a toy expressivity reason non-normalization can avoid sinks, while Softpick supplies a more realistic architecture and evaluation absent here.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
competitive_landscape.difference: StreamingLLM shows that retaining initial sink-token keys and values restores sliding-window generation for up to millions of tokens and that a learned placeholder sink can improve streaming, with up to 22.2x speedup. It establishes practical usefulness but not why sinks are necessary; the present paper supplies one functional necessity mechanism without a streaming experiment.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: attention sinks are a structurally necessary consequence of softmax normalization for trigger-conditional computation rather than an optimization artifact, while ReLU attention can solve the same task without sinks. Prior work already explains sinks through over-mixing control and active-dormant training dynamics, connects them empirically to softmax normalization, analyzes the probability-simplex constraint, and demonstrates gated or non-normalized sink-free architectures. Reviewer inference: the defensible novelty is the first crisp approximation-theoretic necessity theorem for a constructed trigger-conditioned exact-no-op/averaging task, including an all-non-trigger single-layer result, an existential deep pure-attention result, and an explicit zero-loss ReLU separation. It is not a theorem about full modern transformers, multi-head residual models, ordinary language-model objectives, or all attention sinks. The ReLU comparison also depends on explicit prefix-length scaling, so novelty should be described as a normalized-versus-off-state expressivity separation under the stated task, not merely an activation swap.
reviewer_notes: The complete 21-page extraction was read, including the pre/post-trigger proofs, deep unrolling lemmas, explicit ReLU construction, training details, additional 4-layer figures, practical discussion, and related-work appendix. Seven primary arXiv records were independently checked. No numerical table contradiction was found. The central scope tension is explicit: theory covers pure single-head attention compositions, while experiments add multi-head residual models and the title/general discussion refer to softmax transformers broadly. The record therefore preserves theorem quantifiers and labels every extrapolation to real LLMs as reviewer inference rather than proved fact.
